sentences.text: This extinct bird could stand up to 1 meter tall due to its long legs and neck. It possessed a broad, flat bill used for filtering small plants and animals from water, similar to modern dabbling ducks.
The species P. pervetus was duck-sized with longer legs, while P. isoni was larger, exceeding the size of a swan.
The genus Presbyornis was first described by Wetmore in 1926.
Presbyornis was previously known by the synonyms Nautilornis and Coltonia.

Fossil evidence from the Early Eocene Green River Formation suggests Presbyornis nested in colonies and may have died in mass events like volcanism or botulism. Complete skeletons of P. pervetus from the Early Eocene Green River Formation suggest the bird nested in colonies and was vulnerable to botulism.
The genus includes the type species P. pervetus, as well as P. recurvirostra, P. isoni, and the disputed P. mongoliensis.
Specimens attributed to P. mongoliensis from the Early Eocene of Mongolia are fragmentary and likely belong to a stem Phoenicopterimorphae rather than the genus Presbyornis.
Presbyornis belongs to the family Presbyornithidae.

This extinct bird lived in North America during the Late Paleocene and Early Eocene epochs of the Paleogene period. The fossil range of Presbyornis spans from the Late Paleocene to the Early Eocene. Presbyornis lived between 60.9 and 33.9 million years ago, from the Selandian to the Priabonian stages.
